config.title: Graph Valid Tree

intro.title: Graph Valid Tree
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that determines whether a given graph is a valid tree. You will learn the core concept of using Depth-First Search (DFS) to detect cycles and ensure connectivity in an undirected graph. The main technologies involved include JavaScript arrays, objects for adjacency lists, and recursion or iteration for traversal. By the end, you will understand how to apply graph theory fundamentals to solve a common algorithmic lesson.
intro.usecase: The Graph Valid Tree algorithm is essential in network infrastructure and dependency management systems. Network administrators use it to validate that all devices in a corporate network are properly connected without creating loops that could cause broadcast storms. In software build systems, this algorithm ensures dependency graphs form valid trees without circular dependencies that would break compilation. Database administrators apply it to verify that hierarchical data structures maintain proper parent-child relationships without orphaned records or cycles.

objectives: Construct a graph representation using adjacency lists for tree validation
Implement depth-first search to detect cycles in an undirected graph
Apply union-find data structure to check connectivity between nodes
Configure validation logic to ensure all nodes are connected without cycles
Manipulate edge arrays to build and test graph structures
Initialize visited arrays and parent tracking for traversal algorithms
Integrate cycle detection and connectivity checks into a single validation function

content.body: Imagine you're given a set of connections between nodes. How can you tell if they form a valid tree structure without cycles? In this lesson, we'll learn to determine if a graph is a valid tree by exploring its branches from a root node.
content.title: Introduction

content.body:
• Apply tree properties to identify valid tree structures
• Implement a depth-first search to explore branches
• Explain why checking for cycles and connectivity is essential
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Look at this simple graph with 3 nodes connected as 0-1, 1-2. Does this form a valid tree? Think about what makes a tree: connected with no cycles.

content.body: You manually checked connections by following paths, looking for cycles and ensuring all nodes were reachable. This is the core of validating a tree.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When the graph has hundreds of nodes and edges, manually tracing paths becomes impossible. We need a systematic way to explore all branches efficiently.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Think of a tree as exploring branches from a root. We visit nodes level by level or branch by branch, keeping track of where we've been to avoid revisiting (which would mean a cycle).
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Use branch/root visual reasoning; visiting nodes or exploring levels one at a time.

content.body: We can use depth-first search (DFS) starting from any node. As we explore, we check: 1) No cycles (don't revisit nodes except the parent), and 2) All nodes are connected (visited exactly once). If both hold, it's a valid tree.
content.title: The approach
content.visualMetaphor: Show exploring from the root down branches; one level or one branch at a time.

content.body:
1. Build an adjacency list from edges
2. Use DFS to traverse from node 0
3. Track visited nodes to detect cycles
4. Ensure all nodes are visited exactly once
5. Return true if both conditions are met
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Build adjacency list
steps.instruction: Create an adjacency list representation of the graph from the given edges. This will help us easily explore neighbors.
steps.hint: Use an array where each index represents a node, containing an array of its neighbors.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the structure to explore connections.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Remember to add both directions for undirected edges.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. For each edge [u, v], push v to adj[u] and u to adj[v].

steps.title: Initialize visited set
steps.instruction: Create a visited array to track which nodes we've explored. This prevents cycles.
steps.hint: Use a boolean array of size n, initialized to false.
steps.expectedOutcome: Visited array created with n false values
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Now we can track our exploration.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close. Make sure visited has exactly n elements.

steps.title: Define DFS helper
steps.instruction: Create a DFS function that explores branches, checking for cycles by avoiding revisiting nodes (except parent).
steps.hint: The function should take current node and parent node as parameters.
steps.expectedOutcome: DFS that marks visited and checks neighbors
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! You're implementing the branch exploration logic.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start. Remember to handle the parent check and cycle detection.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try: if (neighbor === parent) continue; if (visited[neighbor]) return false; if (!dfs(neighbor, node)) return false;

steps.title: Start DFS and check connectivity
steps.instruction: Call DFS from node 0 and verify that all nodes were visited (graph is connected).
steps.hint: After DFS, check if every element in visited is true.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Well done! You've implemented the complete traversal logic.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Remember to check if DFS returns true and if all nodes are visited.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try: if (!dfs(0, -1)) return false; return visited.every(v => v);

steps.title: Handle edge cases
steps.instruction: Add the final checks: if n === 1 with no edges, and if edges.length !== n-1 (tree property).
steps.hint: A valid tree must have exactly n-1 edges and be connected.
steps.expectedOutcome: Edge cases handled before main logic
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Your solution is now robust and complete.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good. Remember to check both: n === 1 and edges.length === n-1.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try: if (n === 1) return true; if (edges.length !== n - 1) return false;

content.body: You've successfully implemented graph valid tree checking! Remember: a valid tree must be connected with no cycles. We explored branches from a root using DFS, keeping track of visited nodes to detect cycles and ensure all nodes were reached. This approach efficiently handles trees of any size by systematically exploring each branch.
